source_text: Ἰνα δὲ μή τις εἰπῃ τὸ λεγόμενον ὑπὸ τῶν νομιζομένων φιλοσόφων, ὅτι κόμποι καὶ φόβητρά ἐστι τὰ λεγόμενα ὑφ ἡμῶν ὅτι κολάζονται ἐν αἰωνίῳ πυρὶ οἱ ἄδικοι, καὶ διὰ φόβον ἀλλ᾿ οὐ διὰ τὸ καλὸν εἶναι καὶ ἀρεστὸν ἐναρέτως βιοῦν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἀξιοῦμεν, βραχυεπῶς πρὸς τοῦτο ἀποκρινοῦμαι, ὅτι, εἰ μὴ τοῦτό ἐστιν, οὔτε ἔστι θεός, ἤ, εἰ ἔστιν, οὐ μέλει αὐτῷ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, καὶ οὐδέν ἐστιν ἀρετὴ οὐδὲ κακία, καί, ὡς προέφημεν, ἀδίκως τιμωροῦσιν οἱ νομοθέται τοὺς παραβαίνοντας τὰ διατεταγμένα καλά. Ἀλλ᾿ ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἄδικοι ἐκεῖνοι καὶ ὁ αὐτῶν πατήρ, τὰ αὐτὸ αὐτῷ πράττειν διὰ τοῦ λόγου διδάσκων, οἱ τούτοις συντιθέμενοι οὐκ ἄδικοι. Ἐὰν δέ τις τοὺς διαφόρους νόμους τῶν ἀνθρώπων προβάληται, λέγων, ὅτι παρ᾿ οἷς μὲν ἀνθρώποις τάδε καλά, τάδε αἰσχρὰ νενόμισται, παρ᾿ ἄλλοις δὲ τὰ παρ᾿ ἐκείνοις αἰσχρὰ καλά, καὶ τὰ καλὰ αἰσχρὰ νομίζεται, ἀκουέτω καὶ τῶν εἰς τοῦτο λεγομένων. Καὶ νόμους διατάξασθαι τῇ ἑαυτῶν κακίᾳ ὁμοίους τοὺς πονηροὺς ἀγγέλλους ἐπιστάμεθα, οἷς χαίρουσιν οἱ ὅμοιοι γενόμενοι ἄνθρωποι, καὶ ὀρθὸς λόγος παρελθὼν οὐ πάσας δόξας οὐδὲ πάντα δόγματα καλὰ ἀποδείκνυσιν, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν φαῦλα, τὰ δὲ ἀγαθά· ὥστε μοι καὶ πρὸς τοὺς τοιούτους τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ τὰ ὅμοια εἰρήσεται, καὶ λεχθήσεται διὰ πλειόνων, ἐὰν χρεία ᾖ. Τανῦν δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ προκείμενον ἀνέρχομαι.
thought_title: Answering the charge that Christians teach only fear
orientation: Justin is answering the objection of those considered philosophers that Christians use mere boasts and scare-tactics about eternal fire, and he is about to return to his main argument.
pass_a_gloss: But so that no one may say the thing said by those considered philosophers, that the things said by us are boasts and scare-tactics, that the unjust are punished in eternal fire, and that we deem it right for humans to live virtuously because of fear but not because it is good and pleasing, I will answer this briefly, that, if this is not so, either God does not exist, or, if he exists, he does not care for humans, and virtue is nothing and vice is nothing, and, as we said before, lawgivers unjustly punish those who transgress the good things that have been ordained. But since those are not unjust, and their father, teaching through the Word to do the same things as him, those who agree with these are not unjust. But if someone puts forward the differing laws of humans, saying, that among some humans these things are considered good, these things shameful, but among others the things shameful among those are considered good, and the good things are considered shameful, let him hear also the things said to this. And we know that the wicked angels established laws like their own wickedness, in which humans who have become like them rejoice, and right Word, having come, shows not all opinions nor all doctrines to be good, but some bad, some good; so that to me also to such people the same and similar things will be said, and will be said through more, if there is need. But now I go back to the matter set before me.

choices.why: Both nouns are concrete and pejorative; 'scare-tactics' captures φόβητρα as a device for frightening, not just 'fears'.
The adverb modifies the infinitive of living; 'virtuously' keeps the adverbial force rather than turning it into a noun.

choices.english: the good things that have been ordained
choices.why: The participle is passive perfect of διατάσσω, 'ordained' or 'appointed'; 'good things' keeps the neuter plural substantive.
The glossary fixes λόγος as 'Word'; ὀρθός here is 'right' or 'upright', and the phrase refers to Christ as the Word who has come.

choices.english: I go back to the matter set before me
choices.why: ἀνέρχομαι means 'go back up' or 'return'; προκείμενον is the matter laid out or proposed, a standard rhetorical phrase.
rejected: I come to the point at hand

pass_b_english: Some who are considered philosophers say that what we teach is mere boasting and scare tactics: that the unjust are punished in eternal fire, and that we urge people to live virtuously out of fear rather than because it is good and pleasing. So that no one may say this, I will answer briefly. If this is not so, then either there is no God, or, if there is, he does not care about human beings, and virtue and vice are nothing, and, as I said before, lawgivers unjustly punish those who transgress the good things that have been ordained. But since those lawgivers are not unjust, nor is their Father, who teaches through the Word to do the same things as he does, those who agree with them are not unjust either.

But if someone puts forward the differing laws of human beings, saying that among some people certain things are considered good and certain things shameful, while among others the things that are shameful to the first are considered good, and the good things are considered shameful, let him also hear what is said about this. We know that the wicked angels established laws resembling their own wickedness, in which the people who became like them take pleasure. And the right Word, when he came, did not show all opinions and all teachings to be good, but showed some to be worthless and some to be good. So to such people I will say the same and similar things, and they will be said at greater length if there is need. But now I go back to the matter set before me.

problems.quote: the wicked angels established laws resembling their own evil
problems.source_quote: νομοὺς διατάξασθαι τῇ ἑαυτῶν κακίᾳ ὁμοίους τοὺς πονηροὺς ἀγγέλους
problems.why: Source says laws resembling their own wickedness, not their own evil; κακίᾳ is wickedness, not a separate attribute.
problems.fix: the wicked angels established laws resembling their own wickedness
problems.ruling: Greek says laws are arranged similar to wicked angels; translation makes angels the agents establishing laws.

edits.old: the wicked angels established laws resembling their own evil
edits.new: the wicked angels established laws resembling their own wickedness

problems.quote: the right Word, when he came, did not show all opinions and all teachings to be good, but some to be worthless and some to be good.
problems.why: The sentence is grammatically coherent but the logic is confusing: 'did not show all... to be good, but some... to be good' is tautological.
problems.fix: Rephrase: 'did not endorse all opinions, but judged some worthless and some good.'

polish.changed: I restructured the opening sentence so the philosophers' objection comes first and Justin's purpose follows naturally, clarified the logic of the Word's judgment by separating it into its own sentence, and smoothed the rhythm for reading aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.
